readerTitle: The customer asked for glue. She needed a chair that didn't wobble.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (철물점, 사무실 청소 업체, 식자재 유통업체) · 개념 정의는 마케팅 교과서의 표준 구분
insight: 고객의 요청은 문제에 대한 고객 나름의 해결책 추측이다. 요청을 그대로 받기 전에 그 요청이 무엇을 위한 것인지 먼저 찾는다.
misconception: 고객이 원하는 것을 정확히 말해 주니, 요청받은 대로 만들어 주면 고객은 만족한다.

sources.text: Kotler, P. & Armstrong, G. Principles of Marketing: needs, wants and demands의 구분

factChecks.note: Kotler & Armstrong의 정의(니즈는 결핍 상태, 원츠는 문화와 개인 경험이 니즈에 입힌 구체적 형태)를 카드 4에서 쉬운 말로 옮겼습니다. 판본에 따라 표현이 조금 다르니 최신판 문구와 맞는지 확인하세요. 카드에는 교과서 이름을 넣지 않고 "Marketing textbooks"로만 적었습니다.
철물점, 청소 업체, 허브 유통 사례는 모두 가상입니다. 수치 주장은 없고, '30분 정리', '주 2회 추가 방문' 같은 설정만 있습니다. 허브가 며칠 안에 시든다는 표현은 일반적 상식 수준으로 적었습니다.

cards.title: She asked for the strongest glue in the store.
body: A customer walks into a hardware store and asks for the strongest glue you sell. The clerk could point to aisle four. Instead she asks, "What are you fixing?"
A kitchen chair with a wobbly leg. Glue alone won't hold it for long. The customer leaves with two small metal brackets, a few screws and a chair that finally stops wobbling.

image.label: Customer holding glue while a clerk shows a small metal bracket
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 철물점 카운터에서 손님이 큰 접착제 튜브를 들고 있고, 점원이 작은 L자 금속 브래킷을 보여준다. 손님 옆에 다리가 살짝 기운 나무 의자. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A client wants more cleaning.
body: You run an office cleaning company. A good client has you in three times a week. Their office manager emails: "We'd like to move to daily cleaning, starting next month."

options.text: Send a quote for daily cleaning today
options.feedback: Fast, easy and more revenue. But if daily cleaning doesn't fix what's bothering them, they'll pay more and still be unhappy.

options.text: Ask what happened that made them want more cleaning
options.feedback: Your reply is a little slower, but you learn what the request is for. The next card shows what that reveals.

options.text: Suggest they stay at three times a week, since the office isn't that busy
options.feedback: You'd save them money, but you'd be overruling them without knowing why they asked. That can feel like you aren't listening.

cards.title: The request behind the request.
body: The manager explains. Last Tuesday, the CEO walked a visiting client past a messy kitchen. Client visits happen on Tuesdays and Thursdays.

breakdown.label: What they asked for
breakdown.detail: Two extra visits a week, whole office

breakdown.label: What they needed
breakdown.detail: Kitchen and meeting room before visitors arrive

cards.callout: Cheaper for the client than daily cleaning, and it solved the real problem.

cards.title: Needs vs wants
body: A **need** is the problem or goal underneath: to be fed, to stay warm, to impress a visiting client. A **want** is the specific thing a person reaches for to meet it: a burger, a wool coat, daily cleaning.

Marketing textbooks draw this line, and add that wants are shaped by what people have seen before. So customers almost always speak in wants. Their request is their best guess at a solution, not a full description of the problem.

image.label: An iceberg: the request above the water, the need below
image.brief: 빙산 인포그래픽. 물 위의 작은 부분에 "Want: daily cleaning", 물 아래 큰 부분에 "Need: a clean office when clients visit". 깔끔한 플랫 스타일, 파란 계열.

cards.title: Why requests arrive as solutions.
body: Customers aren't being careless. Naming a product is simply faster than describing a problem.
list: **They only know what they've seen.** Nobody asks for an option they've never heard of.
**The request gets passed along.** The manager wrote the email. The CEO had the problem.
**Solutions are easier to say.** "Stronger glue" takes two words. "My chair leg keeps working loose" takes thought.
cards.callout: One question usually finds the need: *What will this let you do?*
cards.softwareNote: Feature requests work the same way. "Add an export-to-spreadsheet button" often means "my boss wants a weekly report." A scheduled email report might meet that need better than the button.

cards.title: One need, many wants. One want, many needs.
body: A need can be met in many ways. A commuter who needs to wake up might buy coffee, tea or an energy drink. Your real competition is everything that meets the same need, not just businesses like yours.

It works the other way too. Two shop owners ask for the same large van. One needs to carry more stock. The other needs to look established to new clients. Same want, different needs, and different things that would make each of them happy.

image.label: One need branching into three products, and one product splitting into two reasons
image.brief: 두 개의 다이어그램 나란히. 왼쪽: "Need to wake up"에서 커피잔, 찻잔, 캔 음료로 갈라지는 화살표. 오른쪽: 승합차 한 대에서 "Carry more stock", "Look established" 두 갈래. 실제 브랜드나 로고 없음.

cards.title: Sometimes the want is the point.
body: Don't treat every request as a puzzle. A mechanic ordering a specific part already knows the need. Questioning them just wastes their time.

Wants also carry meaning. A customer who insists on a certain brand may need what it signals, not only what it does. And meeting the need can mean a smaller sale today, as the cleaning firm found. That usually pays back in trust and loyalty, but not always.

cards.title: Now it's a food distributor.
body: You supply fresh produce to restaurants, delivering every Monday. A bistro asks you to double its weekly order of fresh herbs. You ask why: they run out by Saturday night, their busiest service of the week.

options.text: Double the Monday herb delivery, as asked
options.feedback: It stops the Saturday shortage, but fresh herbs wilt within days. They'll throw away much of what they pay for.

options.text: Keep Monday as it is and add a small Friday delivery
options.feedback: Fresh herbs arrive right before the weekend rush. It costs you an extra stop, so check the order covers that cost.

options.text: Switch them to dried herbs, which last for weeks
options.feedback: It ends the shortage but changes their food. The need is fresh herbs on Saturday, not just any herbs.

cards.title: What customers ask for is their guess at a solution.
body: Before you deliver the request, find out what it's for. The best answer is often cheaper, simpler or different from what they asked.
**Try it today:** take the last three requests from customers. For each, finish the sentence: "They asked for ___ so they could ___."
